::: {.why}
Annualisation looks like a unit conversion and is actually two assumptions, one about the calendar and one about independence, and week 7 is going to abuse the second one badly.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State the two assumptions behind multiplying a daily volatility by the square root of 252, and say which one is empirically false.
- Quantify the error in an annualised volatility from using 252 when the true session count was 250 or 253.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Derive the scaling rule properly: for independent increments the variance of a sum is the sum of variances, so volatility scales with the square root of the horizon. Then write down what happens to that rule when the increments are correlated with lag-one autocorrelation rho, and get the correction factor.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Measure the calendar error with your ten session counts: annualise SPY's daily volatility using each year's true count and using 252, and report the maximum discrepancy in volatility points. It is small. Do it anyway, so that you know it is small and stop worrying about it.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [15 min]{.task-min} Now measure the assumption that is not small: estimate the lag-one autocorrelation of SPY daily returns and of a small-cap name, and apply your correction factor to each annualised volatility. Report the corrected and uncorrected numbers.
:::
:::
